explanation: A former persecutor of Christians who was converted after an encounter with the risen Jesus, known for his journeys and speeches.
The Roman governor who succeeded Felix and heard Paul's defense in Caesarea.
King Herod Agrippa II, a Jewish ruler under Roman rule who was invited to listen to the case against Paul.
The speech or argument presented by an accused person to prove their innocence or justify their actions.
A member of the Jewish people; in this chapter, referring both to the religious tradition and the national roots Paul had before his conversion.
The place where an accused is held during a trial; here, Paul was imprisoned for two years under Felix and Festus.
An supernatural event that breaks natural laws, often used by God to confirm a messenger or message.
The doctrine that Jesus Christ was raised from the dead after his crucifixion, central to Paul's preaching.
The state of being deprived of freedom and held confined by authorities.
